content: Maleic acid, also known as ionized maleate in biological contexts, (Z)-butenedioic acid, cis-butenedioic acid, malenic acid, maleinic acid, or toxilic acid, is an organic compound classified as a dicarboxylic acid. This means it contains two carboxyl (-COOH) groups. Structurally, the molecule consists of an ethylene group flanked by two carboxylic acid groups. Maleic acid represents the cis isomer of butenedioic acid, while its trans isomer is fumaric acid. The physical properties of maleic acid differ significantly from those of fumaric acid. Maleic acid is water-soluble, whereas fumaric acid is not. Additionally, maleic acid has a much lower melting point (130–139°C) compared to fumaric acid (287°C). These differences can be attributed to intramolecular hydrogen bonding in maleic acid, which occurs at the expense of intermolecular interactions. This intramolecular bonding is absent in fumaric acid. It is important to note that maleic acid should not be confused with malic acid or malonic acid, which are distinct types of dicarboxylic acids. In industrial settings, maleic acid is synthesized through the hydrolysis of maleic anhydride. Maleic anhydride itself is produced via the oxidation of benzene or butane. Maleic acid and fumaric acid cannot be interconverted under normal conditions due to the rigidity of the carbon-carbon double bond, which prevents rotation. However, in laboratory settings, the cis isomer (maleic acid) can be converted into the trans isomer (fumaric acid) by exposing it to light and a small amount of bromine. The light generates bromine radicals, which initiate a radical addition reaction with the alkene, forming a bromo-alkane radical. This intermediate allows for single-bond rotation, after which the bromine radicals recombine, resulting in the formation of fumaric acid. In educational demonstrations, maleic acid can be transformed into fumaric acid by heating it in a concentrated hydrochloric acid (12 mol) solution. During this process, the heated maleic acid molecule loses a water molecule, forming an acid anhydride. Upon cooling, the anhydride reabsorbs water but reforms as fumaric acid, the more stable isomer of butenedioic acid. This increased stability arises because the carboxyl groups in fumaric acid are positioned on opposite sides of the molecule, making it non-polar. Consequently, fumaric acid precipitates out of the polar HCl solution, as non-polar solutes are not soluble in polar solvents. In industrial applications, fumaric acid is produced from maleic acid through catalytic isomerization using mineral acids, bromates, or thiourea. The significant difference in water solubility between maleic and fumaric acids facilitates the purification of fumaric acid. Maleic acid serves as an industrial precursor for the production of glyoxylic acid via ozonolysis. It can also be converted into maleic anhydride through dehydration, malic acid through hydration, and succinic acid through hydrogenation. When reacted with thionyl chloride or phosphorus pentachloride, maleic acid forms maleic acid chloride, although isolating the monoacid chloride is not feasible. Additionally, maleic acid is a common reactant in Diels-Alder reactions. The maleate ion is the ionized form of maleic acid and holds significant importance in biochemistry.
